Quantum Transformers

Fault-Tolerant Attention via Quantum Singular Value Transformation

The Central Question

Can quantum computers accelerate transformer attention — and at what cost to QRAM, shots, and circuit depth?

Part 1 — The Classical Transformer

Section divider

jpeg figure

Transformer: Decoder-Only Architecture - Vaswani et al. (2017)

  • Most large language models (GPT, Gemini, Claude) are decoder-only Transformers
  • Each Transformer block contains two sub-blocks:
    • Sub-block 1: Layer Norm → Multi-Head Attention (MHA) → Layer Norm
    • Sub-block 2: Layer Norm → Feed-Forward Network (FFN) → Layer Norm
  • Residual connections bypass each sub-block: output = input + sub-block(input)
  • We assume a single attention head throughout this talk for clarity

Notation

  • S — context length (sequence length)
  • d — embedding dimension (constant across all L layers)
  • L — number of Transformer blocks
  • WQ,WK,WV∈ℝd×d — query, key, value projection matrices
  • WO∈ℝd×d — output projection matrix
  • W1∈ℝ4d×d,W2∈ℝd×4d — FFN weight matrices (expansion factor 4)
  • Memory per block: O(S2d+Sd2) for attention; O(d2) for FFN weights

Classical Attention FLOPs — Derivation

  • Projections Q,K,V: each costs S·d·d=Sd2; total for three: 3Sd2
  • Score matrix QKT: Q∈ℝS×d times KT∈ℝd×S — each of S2 entries is a length-d dot product: cost S2d
  • Softmax: elementwise on S×S — O(S2), subdominant for d>1
  • Context softmax(·)·V: (S×S) times (S×d) — cost S2d
  • Output projection WO: cost Sd2
FLOPsattn=4Sd2+2S2d

Attention FLOPs: Two Regimes

FLOPsattn=4Sd2⏟projection cost+2S2d⏟score cost
  • 4Sd2 dominates when d≫S: wide model, short context
  • 2S2d dominates when S≫d: long context — the regime quantum attention targets
  • Crossover at S=2d: for GPT-3 (d=12,288) this is S≈24,600 tokens
  • Modern LLMs with S=128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens are deep in the S2d regime

FFN FLOPs: Pure Quadratic in d, Linear in S

FLOPsFFN=8Sd2
  • The expansion factor 4 appears twice (d→4d then 4d→d), giving the factor of 8
  • No S2 term — FFN cost grows with S only linearly; attention grows quadratically
  • Full block: FLOPsblock=12Sd2+2S2d; over L layers: L(12Sd2+2S2d)
  • Layer Norm costs O(Sd) per block — negligible for large d

Part 2 — Quantum Computing Eras

Section divider

From NISQ to Full Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing

timeline
  title Quantum Computing Era Roadmap
  section NISQ (2016 onward)
    Noisy qubits : Circuit depth constrained by decoherence
    50 to 1000 physical qubits : No logical error correction
  section Early FTQC (2023 onward)
    First logical qubits : Surface codes, distance 3 to 7
    ~1000 physical per logical qubit : 10 to 20 logical qubits
  section Full FTQC (2028 onward)
    Logical error rate ~1e-15 : Unlimited circuit depth
    Shor factoring and large QPE : Quantum Transformers enabled

NISQ — Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum

  • Qubits affected by noise: gate errors ~0.5–1% per 2-qubit gate, readout errors, cross-talk
  • Circuit depth is constrained — decoherence limits depth before qubits lose their quantum state
  • Error mitigation (not correction): ZNE, PEC, dynamical decoupling — bridge strategies that do not scale to deep circuits
  • Quantum advantage unproven — tensor networks can often match NISQ results for the shallow circuits that NISQ hardware can reliably execute
  • Key consequence: complex algorithms like Transformers require depth that NISQ cannot support

FTQC — Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing

  • Logical qubits backed by many physical qubits via error-correcting codes (e.g., surface code)
  • Logical error rate ~10−15 — effectively noiseless; circuit depth is unconstrained
  • T-gate count is the primary cost metric — T gates require expensive magic-state distillation
  • Hardware threshold: requires physical error rate below ~10−3; Google Willow (2024) demonstrated below-threshold operation with 105 qubits
  • Scale needed for useful algorithms: >100,000 physical qubits for Shor's at practically relevant key sizes

Physical Qubit Count Over Time — IBM, Google, D-Wave

IBM Heron: Deliberate Regression Reveals the Real Metric

  • IBM Condor (2023) reached 1,121 physical qubits — peak raw qubit count
  • IBM Heron (current): 133–156 qubits — a deliberate step backward in count
  • Why regress? Gate fidelity and modularity matter more than raw qubit count:
    • Heron achieves lower error rates and better error-correction potential per qubit
    • Condor's qubit count was not matched by error rates useful for building logical qubits
  • The lesson: the relevant metric shifted from qubit count to logical qubit count — which requires high fidelity, not just high count

Part 3 — Block Encoding: Embedding Non-Unitary Matrices

Section divider

The Fundamental Problem — Quantum Gates Must Be Unitary

  • A quantum gate U acting on n qubits must be unitary: U†U=I
  • Matrices of interest — attention weights, FFN weight matrices W1,W2 — are not unitary
  • Solution: embed A into the top-left corner of a larger unitary UA:
(⟨0|⊗a⊗In)UA(|0⟩⊗a⊗In)=Aα
  • a = number of ancilla qubits; α≥‖A‖ is the subnormalization factor
  • Subnormalization ensures all singular values of A/α lie in [0,1] — the valid quantum amplitude range
  • Post-selection: measuring ancilla =|0⟩ collapses the system register to A|ψ⟩/α

Case 0 — When A Is Unitary, No Embedding Needed

Adding Ancilla Qubits Expands the Hilbert Space

  • When A is non-unitary, we must embed it into a larger unitary UA by adding ancilla qubits
  • Each ancilla qubit doubles the total Hilbert space: n system qubits + a ancilla qubits → matrix size 2n+a×2n+a
  • A/α occupies only the top-left 2n×2n corner — the rest of UA is filled to enforce unitarity
  • Post-selecting the ancilla on |0⟩ projects onto that top-left corner, effectively applying A/α

Case a=1 — One Ancilla Qubit Doubles the Hilbert Space

Case a=2 — Two Ancilla Qubits Give a 4·2^n Unitary

Why More Ancilla Qubits? Three Concrete Reasons

  • 1. Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU): if A=∑k=0L−1λkUk, you need ⌈log2L⌉ ancillae to index terms — 100 Pauli terms require 7 ancillae
  • 2. Subnormalization α<1: each halving of α costs roughly one more ancilla qubit
  • 3. Sparse oracle encodings: a d-sparse matrix needs O(logN+logd) ancillae to address nonzero entries
  • Practical range: a=1 is the theoretical floor; real algorithms use a=5–15, multiplying Hilbert space by 2a (factor 32 to 32,768)
  • Cost metric: α controls computational cost — circuit repetitions and QSVT overhead

Block-Encoding Circuit: Low-Level Gates and the Unitary Embedding

Part 4 — Shots: Sampling Quantum Outputs

Section divider

Why Shots Are Necessary — Quantum Measurement Is Probabilistic

  • Measuring |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1⟩ yields 0 with probability |α|2 and 1 with probability |β|2; the state is destroyed
  • You must re-run the circuit to reconstruct the distribution — this is not a hardware limitation, it is a law of quantum mechanics
SNISQ=Sstats×Snoise mitigation,SFTQC=Sstats
  • FTQC eliminates the noise-mitigation tax; the statistical floor remains in both eras

Anatomy of Shots: NISQ vs FTQC

The Statistical Floor — Hoeffding Bound

  • For a k-qubit system, estimating output probabilities to precision ε with confidence 1−δ:
S≥12ε2ln(2δ)
  • Independent of qubit count — asking "did the 64-qubit algorithm output the right answer?" costs the same shots as a 1-qubit experiment asking the same binary question
  • For ε=0.03, δ=0.01: S≈2,800 shots regardless of system size
  • Full state tomography is the exception: recovering all 2k amplitudes costs O(2k/ε2) — exponential and infeasible at scale

Hoeffding Bound: Shots Scale with the Question, Not the System

Shots in Practice: NISQ Explodes, FTQC Stays Flat

  • 1 qubit (Hadamard + measure): NISQ ~5,000 shots (statistics + modest mitigation); FTQC ~3,000 (statistics only)
  • 4 qubits (GHZ state): NISQ ~50,000 shots — noise leaks probability across all 16 bitstrings, forcing heavy mitigation; FTQC ~2,000
  • 64 qubits (deep algorithm): NISQ — intractable; error mitigation overhead becomes exponential in circuit depth; FTQC ~40 shots for a high-probability-output algorithm (Shor's, QPE)
  • Key point: NISQ shot count grows with qubit count because noise accumulates; FTQC stays near the statistical floor

Part 5 — From Classical SVD to QSVD

Section divider

Classical SVD — The Geometric Foundation

  • Every matrix A∈ℂm×n admits:
A=UΣV†
  • U, V unitary (rotations); Σ diagonal with singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr≥0
  • Geometric reading: V† rotates input to right singular vector basis; Σ stretches along those axes; U rotates result to output basis
  • Key insight: the singular values {σi} are the intrinsic amplitudes of the transformation — basis-independent and encoding all scaling information
  • Why target singular values? Low-rank approximation, pseudoinverse, and attention scores are all functions of {σi}

SVD as Three Geometric Stages: Rotate, Stretch, Rotate

Why Singular Values Are the Right Quantum Target

  • Low-rank approximation: keep only the k largest singular values — best rank-k approximation (Eckart–Young)
  • Pseudoinverse: A+=VΣ+U† — replace each σi with 1/σi for nonzero values
  • Attention scores QKT have a natural SVD — singular values encode the strength of each attention pattern
  • Quantum advantage target: rather than computing A explicitly at cost O(S2d), apply a polynomial function p(Σ) to all singular values simultaneously in O(polylog) depth

Block Encoding Enables QSVT — The Key Identity

(⟨0|⊗a⊗In)UA(|0⟩⊗a⊗In)=Aα
  • UA is a unitary — a valid quantum gate on n+a qubits
  • α≥‖A‖ ensures singular values of A/α lie in [0,1]
  • Post-selecting ancilla on |0⟩: system register holds A|ψ⟩/α
  • Success probability: ~1/α2 — amplitude amplification boosts to O(1) at cost O(α)
  • Circuit size: for d-sparse A, compile UA in O(d·poly(logN)) T-gates — exponentially fewer than N2 entries

Block Encoding Circuit: Post-Selection Extracts A/α

QSP Theorem — Polynomial Functions on Singular Values

  • QSP Theorem: by interleaving UA with single-qubit phase rotations {eiϕkZ}, any odd or even polynomial p(σ) with |p(σ)|≤1 on [−1,1] is applied to all singular values simultaneously
  • Phase angles {ϕk} are pre-computed classically (tools: QSPPACK, pyqsp) — the compilation step
  • Circuit depth: O(dpoly) where dpoly is the polynomial degree
  • QSVT generalizes QSP to the full two-register setting: implements p(Σ) coherently
QSVT of degree d implements p(Σ) in O(d) block-encoded oracle calls

QSVT Circuit: Phase Rotations Interleaved with U_A

QSVD and the GUO Dependency Chain

  • QSVD uses QSVT with p(σ) designed to project onto singular vectors — producing coherent states |vi⟩, |ui⟩ weighted by singular values
  • The complete dependency chain:
    • Classical SVD → singular values {σi} are intrinsic amplitudes
      • Block encoding → embeds A/α in unitary UA; post-selection extracts A|ψ⟩/α
        • QSP → phase rotations implement any bounded polynomial p(σ) on all σi in O(d) depth
          • QSVT → two-register generalization implementing p(Σ) coherently
            • QSVD → project onto singular vectors via QSVT
              • GUO Transformer → Chebyshev approx of softmax via QSVT on QKT/d

Part 6 — Poly-Logarithmic Depth: Why Analytic Functions Win

Section divider

What O(polylog(1/ε)) Means

  • The claim: QSVT approximates smooth functions to precision ε with circuit depth dpoly=O(logk(1/ε))
  • Not O(1/ε) or O(1/ε2) — depth grows only logarithmically as ε→0
  • For ε=10−6:
    • O(1/ε2)=1012 — infeasible
    • O(1/ε)=106 — infeasible
    • O(log(1/ε))≈14 — trivially feasible
  • Key condition: the target function must be analytic (not merely smooth) on [−1,1]

Link 1 — Circuit Depth Equals Polynomial Degree

  • In a QSP circuit with phase angles {ϕ1,…,ϕd}, the circuit implements a degree-d polynomial:
dcircuit=dpoly
  • The question reduces to: how high a degree polynomial approximates the target function to precision ε?
  • This is a classical question from approximation theory — independent of quantum mechanics
  • The answer depends entirely on the analyticity of the target function, not on the domain size or qubit count

Link 2 — Chebyshev Approximation: Analytic Functions Converge Exponentially

  • Smooth function on [−1,1]: best degree-d Chebyshev approximation satisfies:
‖f−pd‖∞≤C·Mkdk(algebraic convergence)
  • Analytic function (analytic on a complex strip containing [−1,1]): convergence is exponential in d:
‖f−pd‖∞≤C·r−d,r>1
  • Softmax involves eσ — entire (analytic on all of ℂ), so r>1 can be large, giving very fast convergence

Link 3 — Inverting for Degree d

  • Set C·r−d≤ε and solve:
r−d≤εC⟹−dlogr≤log(εC)⟹d≥log(C/ε)logr d=O(log(1/ε))
  • For GELU and softmax (entire functions), this is O(polylog(1/ε)) with exponent k=1
  • Caveat: the constant hidden in O(·) includes α from block encoding — often large and frequently suppressed in complexity claims

Analyticity determines whether the algorithm is computationally feasible.

Activation Choice Is Not Cosmetic — It Determines Feasibility

  • GELU: GELU(x)=x·Φ(x) — entire function; degree d=O(log(1/ε))
  • Softmax: involves eσ — entire; degree d=O(log(1/ε))
  • ReLU: ReLU(x)=(x+|x|)/2 — involves |x| which is not analytic at x=0:
\||x|−pd(x)\|∞≤O(1/d)⇒d=O(1/ε) for ReLU
  • At ε=10−3: GELU needs depth ≈10; ReLU needs depth 103 — three orders of magnitude more

Part 7 — GUO Quantum Transformer Architecture

Section divider

Classical Attention — The Target Formula

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)V
  • Q,K,V∈ℝS×d
  • Score matrix QKT∈ℝS×S has a natural SVD — singular values encode attention pattern strengths
  • Classical cost: O(S2d) — quadratic in context length
  • Quantum target: QSVT circuit of depth O(polylog(Sd)) under QRAM + sparsity assumptions

Classical vs Quantum Attention at a Glance

  • Classical cost is quadratic in S — the bottleneck for long-context LLMs
  • Quantum cost is poly-logarithmic in S — under QRAM and sparsity assumptions
  • Every stage of the quantum pipeline requires a block-encoded oracle call
  • The five-stage GUO pipeline maps exactly to the classical five operations

Stage 1 — Data Loading: The QRAM Bottleneck

  • Quantum amplitude encoding of 𝐪i∈ℝd:
|𝐪i⟩=1‖𝐪i‖∑j=0d−1qij|j⟩
  • Naive loading: requires O(d) operations — destroys the poly-log speedup
  • QRAM: hardware tree structure that queries memory in O(logd) parallel time using O(d) circuit elements
  • Reality: QRAM hardware does not exist at scale; highly sensitive to decoherence; error-correction requirements enormous
  • Without QRAM: readin is O(d) or O(S) — and the end-to-end speedup vanishes

Stages 2–3 — Block-Encode QK^T, Apply Softmax via QSVT

  • Stage 2: construct UA such that ⟨0|⊗aUA|0⟩⊗a=QKT/(αdk)
    • d-sparse attention: O(d·poly(logS)) T-gates
    • Dense attention (d=S): partially negates the quantum advantage
  • Stage 3: softmax via QSVT — eσ is entire so:
dpoly=O(log(1/ε))

The QSVT circuit of depth dpoly applies the Chebyshev approximation of softmax to every singular value simultaneously

Stages 4–5 — Multiply by V and Measurement

  • Stage 4: second block-encoded QSVT applies V — total depth O(dsoftmax·dmult), both poly-logarithmic
  • Stage 5 — measurement dilemma:
    • Sample: O(1/ε2) shots per token, times S tokens — total O(S/ε2) shots for full output
    • Maintain coherence: feed each block's output directly into the next as a quantum state — avoids readout cost, but T-gate count grows as O(L·dpoly·Tgate(UA))
  • LayerNorm problem: classical cost O(Sd) and negligible; quantum implementation requires nonlinear operations (mean, variance, normalize) on amplitude-encoded states — does not fit QSVT; unsolved

GUO Quantum Transformer Pipeline

graph LR
  A["Q, K, V in R^(S x d)"] --> B["Stage 1: QRAM Loading\nO(log d) per query\nDominant assumption"]
  B --> C["Stage 2: Block-Encode QK^T\nd-sparse: O(d polylog S) T-gates"]
  C --> D["Stage 3: QSVT Softmax\ndepth O(log 1/eps)\nChebyshev poly of exp"]

Part 8 — Complete Cost Model

Section divider

Four Cost Components — All Must Be Accounted For

  • The literature typically quotes circuit evaluation cost only — the most optimistic number
  • Complete cost = Readin × Shots × Circuit evaluation, plus Readout
    1. Readin: loading classical data into quantum superposition — QRAM dependent
    2. Readout: extracting classical results — no-cloning limits what is extractable
    3. Shots: number of circuit repetitions — Hoeffding or reliability bound
    4. Circuit evaluation: T-gate count per shot — poly-log depth times T-gates per oracle call

Cost 1 — Readin: The QRAM Problem

  • Loading 𝐱∈ℝN into |ψ⟩=∑ixi|i⟩ naively requires O(N) operations
  • QRAM proposed: QRAM:∑iαi|i⟩|0⟩→∑iαi|i⟩|xi⟩ in O(logN) time
  • Reality: no large-scale QRAM prototype; every tree node is a decoherence source; error-correction requirements orders of magnitude beyond current capability
  • Every quantum ML speedup claim that beats classical methods is load-bearing on QRAM — without it, readin is O(N) and the speedup vanishes

Cost 2 — Readout: The No-Cloning Barrier

  • One measurement of |ψ⟩=∑iαi|i⟩ yields one sample from {|αi|2} — destroys the state
  • Full state tomography costs O(N/ε2) — exponential in register size, infeasible at scale
  • Practical readout types:
    • Single bitstring (Shor's, Grover's): ≈40 shots for failure prob δ=10−12
    • Expectation value ⟨O⟩: Hoeffding gives O(1/ε2) shots
    • Full token distribution (V≈100,000): O(V) shots — quantum transformer must sample, not return the full distribution

S≥12ε2ln(2δ)

Costcircuit=dpoly×Tgate(UA)=O(log(1/ε)·d·poly(logS))
  • Compare to classical O(S2d) — quantum wins only if QRAM available, attention d-sparse, and shot overhead manageable

Part 9 — Quantum FFN: Full Treatment

Section divider

Classical FFN — Two Linear Layers with Nonlinear Activation

FFN(𝐱)=W2σ(W1𝐱+𝐛1)+𝐛2,W1∈ℝ4d×d,W2∈ℝd×4d
  • Cost per token: 4d2 (first layer) + O(d) (activation) + 4d2 (second layer) =O(d2)
  • Over S tokens: FLOPsFFN=8Sd2 — no S2 term
  • FFN dominates total cost only when d≫S/4 — not the case for modern LLMs with long context
  • Quantum target: replace O(d2) per token with O(polylogd) under QRAM + bounded-α

Step 1 — Block-Encoding W1 and W2

UW1:(⟨0|⊗a1⊗In)UW1(|0⟩⊗a1⊗In)=W1α1
  • α1≥‖W1‖; a1=⌈log2α1⌉ ancilla qubits; analogously α2,UW2 for W2
  • Trained weight matrices have bounded spectral norm by implicit regularization: α=O(poly(d)), contributing O(logd) ancillae
  • Dense 4d×d matrices (s=d): O(d·poly(logd)) T-gates per application

Step 2 — Activation via QSVT: Spectral vs Elementwise

  • Softmax in attention acts on singular values of the score matrix — exactly the QSVT spectral setting
  • The FFN activation σ acts elementwise on the post-linear vector — a different primitive
  • Solution: embed elementwise operation as diagonal matrix D=diag(c0,c1,…,cd−1)
    • Singular values of D are precisely |ci|, so QSVT applies directly
    • GELU: entire function; dGELU=O(log(1/ε))
    • ReLU: involves |x|, not analytic at 0; dReLU=O(1/ε)

Step 3 — Sequential Composition and Amplitude Amplification

  • Three sequential QSVT circuits: UW1, then Uσ, then UW2
  • Each post-selection succeeds with probability ~1/α2; three sequential post-selections compound:
P(success)~1α12·ασ2·α22
  • Amplitude amplification (Grover reflections) boosts to O(1) at cost O(α) extra circuit repetitions:
TFFN=O(α1·ασ·α2·log(1/ε)·poly(logd))
  • The α factors are the "hidden constants" that complexity analyses routinely suppress

Step 4 — Bias Terms via LCU

  • Classical affine map 𝐱↦W𝐱+𝐛 must be block-encoded
  • LCU technique: W𝐱+𝐛=∑kλkUk|ψ⟩
  • Requires ⌈log2L⌉ ancillae to index L terms; adds ‖λ‖1=∑k|λk| to subnormalization
  • For bias addition: L=2 terms — mild overhead, but a real contribution to ancilla count and total α

FFN QSVT Circuit: Weight Matrices Flanking QSVT Activation

Three FFN-Specific Caveats

  • 1. Activation choice is load-bearing: GELU gives O(log(1/ε)) depth; ReLU gives O(1/ε) — at ε=10−3 that is three orders of magnitude inflation. Any quantum FFN claim must specify which activation and justify it.
  • 2. Weight matrices change during training: recompiling UW1 after each gradient step requires recomputing QSVT phase angles (via QSPPACK/pyqsp). Training a quantum transformer is almost entirely an open problem.
  • 3. Intermediate states cannot be cloned: between W1 and W2, intermediate activations exist only as quantum states — inspecting, storing, or differentiating them requires measurement, which collapses the state. Backpropagation through quantum circuits has no settled solution at scale.

Part 10 — Critical Caveats and Open Problems

Section divider

Caveat 1 — QRAM Is Load-Bearing and Speculative

  • The O(polylog(Sd)) speedup depends entirely on QRAM loading data in O(logN) time
  • Without QRAM, readin costs O(N) and the speedup vanishes — this is not a footnote, it is the entire argument
  • Dequantization (Ewin Tang, 2018): many quantum linear algebra speedups can be matched classically with sample-and-query access — the conditions that enable QRAM also enable classical dequantization
  • GUO's result needs rigorous analysis to show it is not dequantizable via Tang-style classical algorithms

Caveat 2 — Hidden Constants and Subnormalization

  • Every O(polylog) claim hides the product α1·ασ·α2 from block encoding
  • For attention: α≥‖QKT/dk‖ — can be O(Sd) in the worst case
  • Example: if α=O(S1/2) and dpoly=O(log(1/ε)), the actual T-gate cost is O(S1/2log(1/ε)·poly(logS)) — better than classical O(S2) but not O(polylogS)
  • Honest speedup claims must report α explicitly and verify it is bounded by O(polylog)

Open Problems in Quantum Transformers

  • LayerNorm: classical O(Sd), negligible; quantum requires nonlinear operations (mean, variance, normalize) on amplitude-encoded states — does not fit the QSVT spectral framework; genuinely unsolved
  • Backpropagation: intermediate activations as quantum states cannot be inspected or differentiated without measurement; quantum gradient descent at transformer scale has no settled solution
  • QRAM hardware: enabling assumption for all quantum ML speedup claims; no large-scale prototype; fundamental decoherence obstacles remain
  • Multi-head attention: the GUO analysis assumes a single head; multi-head introduces additional structure not fully characterized
  • Dequantization check: rigorous analysis of whether GUO's result is susceptible to Tang-style classical speedup

Summary — Quantum Transformers: What We Know

  • Classical baseline: attention FLOPs =4Sd2+2S2d per layer; for modern LLMs the S2d term dominates heavily
  • Quantum engine: QSVT applies any bounded polynomial to all singular values in O(dpoly) depth; analytic functions (GELU, softmax) achieve dpoly=O(log(1/ε))
  • End-to-end speedup claim: O(S2d)→O(polylog(Sd)) under QRAM + sparse attention + FTQC + bounded α
  • Three caveats: QRAM is speculative; α hides potentially large constants; dequantization may recover the speedup classically
  • Open: LayerNorm, backpropagation, QRAM hardware, multi-head analysis
  • Bottom line: beautiful mathematics with exponential potential — but every load-bearing assumption needs independent verification
